title: The Axis of Upheaval Goes to War
gist: Kendall-Taylor and Fontaine argue that Russia, China, Iran and North Korea have turned their Ukraine-war cooperation into a networked system now helping Iran against the US, while Trump-era friction strains America's far larger alliance network. They urge Washington to stop undercutting allies and strengthen its own network for a long contest.

insights.claim: Chinese entities supplied Iran high-resolution satellite imagery of Muwaffaq Salti Air Base before the July 17 Iranian missile strike that killed three American soldiers, and later imagery that may have helped assess damage.
insights.speaker: Andrea Kendall-Taylor
insights.so_what: Evidence of Chinese indirect military support to Iran raises US-China escalation and sanctions risk.

insights.claim: Russia aided Iranian targeting: 14 Russian spy satellites passed over Prince Sultan Air Base two days before the March 27 attack that wounded 12 Americans, US officials concluded Moscow fed Iran satellite intelligence, and Russian engineers are helping Iran develop supersonic cruise missiles.
insights.speaker: Andrea Kendall-Taylor
insights.so_what: Russian-Iranian military technology transfer worsens the threat to US forces and Gulf assets.

insights.claim: Russia and China have helped Iran without entering the war directly, by providing intelligence, technology and components, and economic and diplomatic support, and this restraint is a defining feature of how the partnerships work rather than a sign of weakness.
insights.speaker: Andrea Kendall-Taylor
insights.so_what: Expect continued bounded support, so escalation to direct confrontation is less likely than indirect proxy-style assistance.

insights.claim: Axis cooperation has shifted from bilateral transactions focused on Russia's war to a network in which innovations circulate: Russia's improved Shahed-derived, jet-powered Geran drones flow back to Iran, North Korea and China, which gain production know-how and combat lessons.
insights.speaker: Andrea Kendall-Taylor
insights.so_what: Drone-technology diffusion means faster, harder-to-intercept drones may soon appear against US forces and regional energy infrastructure.

insights.claim: Conflict in one theater creates gains for partners elsewhere: Iran's closure of the Strait of Hormuz sent oil prices soaring, giving Russia a windfall and prompting Washington to temporarily ease restrictions on Russian oil exports.
insights.speaker: Andrea Kendall-Taylor
insights.so_what: Hormuz disruption transfers revenue to Russia and weakens sanctions leverage, a link to watch in oil markets.

insights.claim: US redeployment of air and missile defenses and two aircraft carriers to the Middle East left none in the Indo-Pacific, giving China operational freedom and lowering its vulnerability to depleted US munition stocks, advantages that could last years if Washington settles into prolonged containment of Iran.
insights.speaker: Andrea Kendall-Taylor
insights.so_what: The Middle East commitment thins deterrence in the western Pacific, a Taiwan-risk factor.

insights.claim: The US capture of Venezuelan leader Nicolas Maduro and the killing of Iranian Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei reinforced fears in Beijing, Moscow, Pyongyang and Tehran about US intervention and regime security, keeping the axis motivated.
insights.speaker: Andrea Kendall-Taylor
insights.so_what: Regime-security fear is the glue, so US outreach to peel members away is unlikely to work.

insights.claim: The US entered the conflict with a vastly larger network of allies and bases, yet many traditional partners were reluctant to associate with the campaign, denied some military access for a time, and publicly resisted calls to help secure the Strait of Hormuz.
insights.speaker: Andrea Kendall-Taylor
insights.so_what: Allied reluctance limits US operational options and may raise shipping and energy risk.

insights.claim: Trump administration actions strengthen the axis and weaken allied cohesion, including offering to sell Beijing weapons while stalling Taiwan arms sales, favoring Kim Jong Un over South Korea's president, pressuring Ukraine, threatening to bomb Oman, and imposing tariffs on allies.
insights.speaker: Andrea Kendall-Taylor
insights.so_what: The authors see US policy as eroding the network advantage; track allied hedging and defense-industrial realignment.

insights.claim: Washington should strengthen supply chains through trusted partners, share technology and encourage allies to take on more security burdens, but not transfer defense responsibilities faster than allies can develop capabilities.
insights.speaker: Andrea Kendall-Taylor
insights.so_what: Burden-shifting done too fast makes the coalition individually stronger but collectively less effective.

insights.claim: The contest between networks will be nearly global and long, and as the unsuccessful regime-change effort in Iran showed, there are no shortcuts to besting the axis countries.
insights.speaker: Andrea Kendall-Taylor
insights.so_what: Plan for a protracted competition, with sustained defense and sanctions-related policy implications.
